scenes.name: Reggae roots y dub
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Junto al funk, la otra gran lección rítmica del postpunk: el bajo como protagonista, el espacio y el eco de la producción dub. Las técnicas de estudio de Jamaica (King Tubby, Lee Perry) se convierten en herramienta de vanguardia para PiL, The Slits, The Pop Group y On-U Sound.
scenes.family: Ritmos negros: dub, funk, disco y hip hop

podcast.title: Association with The Clash
podcast.body: Don Letts was a confidant and friend to both the Sex Pistols and The Clash, later becoming a member of Big Audio Dynamite alongside his Clash bandmate, Mick Jones. "Don Letts, a confidant and friend of both the sex pistols and the clash... And later on, Don would become a member of Big Audio Dynamite with this clash buddy, Mick Jones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneer DJ in Early Punk Scene
podcast.body: Don Letts, a member of Big Audio Dynamite with Mick Jones of The Clash, was deeply involved in the early punk scene as a DJ. He played dub and reggae records in clubs, introducing these new genres and sounds to the pioneers of the punk era, marking a significant first in musical cross-pollination. "And he got involved in the early punk scene as a DJ spinning dub and reggae records in clubs, introducing that music to pioneers in the punk era to New genres."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Punk and Reggae Crossover
podcast.body: In the 1970s, Don Letts was a DJ who played a crucial role in introducing reggae and dub music to a new generation of punk kids in clubs. At a time when punk records were scarce, Jamaican music, including dub and other Black music forms, became the foundational sound for these punks until their own genre's records emerged. "Don Letts, a confidant and friend of both the sex pistols and the clash. He was the DJ who introduced reggae and dub to a new generation of these punk kids in the 1970s in clubs where they hung out. See, there were no punk records yet, so that music, Jamaican music, dub music, black music became theirs until they had some punk records to listen to."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band Lifespan Template Adherence
xref.body: The Clash is cited as a band that closely followed Don Letts' theory on the average useful lifespan of a band, which typically involves a period of intense activity, a peak around year four or five, and then an inevitable decline due to internal and external conflicts. "Now the clash certainly followed that template, sort of the Beatles and the Smiths."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band Lifespan Template and Dramatic End
xref.body: Nirvana followed Don Letts' band lifespan template "right on schedule," suggesting their career trajectory mirrored the typical rise, peak, and fall within a seven-to-eight-year span, until lead singer Kurt Cobain "ended things rather dramatically." "And Nirvana was right on schedule until Kurt ended things rather dramatically."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Sloan In Their Own Words: Part 1

xref.title: Don Letts' Theory Connection
xref.body: Don Letts, a British DJ and filmmaker close to The Clash during the original punk scene, developed a theory that the optimal lifespan for most bands is seven to nine years. He suggests that this period allows for birth, rise, peak, and then explosion due to internal pressures like creative differences. The Clash are cited as an example of a brilliant band for their time that, despite multi-million dollar offers, never reunited to record new material. "He was especially close with the clash. And he has a theory. He believes the average and proper lifespan of most bands is seven years, nine at the outside."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exceptional Longevity
xref.body: Pearl Jam is highlighted as an exception to Don Letts' theory on band lifespan, having continuously existed since 1991, demonstrating a sustained career well beyond the typical seven or eight years predicted. "Pearl Jam. They've existed since 1991."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exceptional Longevity
xref.body: The Cure is highlighted as an exception to Don Letts' theory on band lifespan, having been active since 1976, similar to U2, demonstrating a sustained career far beyond the typical seven or eight years. "U2 has been around since 1976, same with the Cure."

xref.title: Rage's Lifespan Aligns with Don Letts' Theory
xref.body: Rage Against the Machine formed in 1991 and broke up in 2000, lasting approximately nine years. This timeframe aligns with British DJ and filmmaker Don Letts' theory that the average lifespan of most bands is seven to nine years, after which they typically "explode" due to internal pressures like creative differences and diverging lifestyles. "They formed in 1991, got big real fast, and right on schedule, they broke up in 2000, torn apart by a series of internal conflicts."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
